adversarial_test_results.prompt: The estate office keeps a leather-bound survey book that records the layout of the northern property in considerable detail. The first pages hold a sketch of the boundary wall, which runs for nine hundred metres from the eastern gate to the stone bridge at the foot of the hill. From that bridge the wall turns north and follows a low ridge for six hundred metres before it reaches the edge of the woods. The surveyor calculated that the enclosed area comes to roughly forty hectares, of which about a third is arable land and the remainder grazing pasture. He measured the height of the ridge at three places with a tape and a spirit level, and entered the results in the margin: eleven metres at the eastern end, nineteen in the middle, and fourteen where the ridge meets the trees. Breadths were entered the same way, with the narrowest section of the wall about sixty centimetres at the base and the rest a good deal heavier. The two barns stand separately, one near the gate and one behind the kitchen garden, with a paved yard between them. The yard measures thirty paces on each side. Inside the main barn the roof rises sharply, and the distance from the floor to the highest beam is close to nine metres. A loft covers the western half of the interior, and a ladder gives access to it. The book describes the drainage next as a serious problem: several hundred metres of clay pipe were laid in the eighteen nineties and many of the joints have since collapsed. Water collects in the lower field after heavy rain and stands there for a week at a time. The surveyor recommended replacing the worst sections with plastic pipe of a similar bore and adding a soakaway at the bottom of the slope. A second problem was the track that leads from the road to the yard. It is barely three metres broad for most of its length, and it turns sharply where it passes the orchard, so that a lorry has trouble getting round the corner. The surveyor proposed making the bend broader and laying a strip of gravel on the steepest part. The final pages list the trees, with the age of each estimated from the girth of its trunk. The oldest oak has a girth of six metres and a crown that covers most of the southern lawn. Its shadow falls over the greenhouse for much of the afternoon in summer. A line of limes borders the drive, and their crowns meet overhead to form a tunnel of leaves. The book ends with a summary of the weights carried by the bridge, which was rebuilt in nineteen hundred and ten and strengthened sixty years later. The new deck was tested with a load of twenty tonnes, applied in stages, and it deflected by less than a centimetre at the centre. In a loose sleeve at the back of the book are the receipts for the repairs, together with a letter from the tenant complaining that the eastern gate is weak. The gate was replaced the following spring with one of oak, hung on iron hinges and painted dark green. Its posts were set in concrete to a depth of a metre. The tenant also asked for a new hedge on the boundary with the road, since the old one had gaps where sheep had pushed through. Hawthorn was planted in a double row, and the plants were spaced half a metre from each other and protected with plastic sleeves. The hedge needed three seasons to fill out, and by the fourth it was dense enough to turn a wind. The surveyor added a short paragraph of his own at the end, in which he admitted that the figures in the book were probably accurate to a few centimetres and that anyone building on the property should measure the ground again before cutting timber or laying foundations.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long survey passage dense with extent and magnitude content (metres, hectares, height, distance, weight) but built only from words the hypothesis says stay near zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The village hall committee meets on the first Tuesday of each month, and for most of the year the agenda is short. Reports are read, minor repairs are approved, and the meeting closes before nine. This autumn was different. The parish council had announced that the roof of the hall would be replaced before winter, and every society that used the building was asked to move its equipment into the old dairy for the duration of the work. The book club went first. Its members carried crates of paperbacks down the lane in the rain, stacking them on pallets that the tenant had left by the gate. Then came the amateur dramatic society, which had stored costumes, backdrops and a piano in the store room since the nineteen seventies. The piano was the difficulty. It was an upright of considerable weight and it had to come out through the double doors at the side of the hall, which meant removing one of the doors from its hinges. Two men from the garage next door did this with a screwdriver and a good deal of patience. The choir followed on the following Saturday. Their music had been kept in filing cabinets, and the cabinets were empty, light and easy to shift. Tea was served in the yard afterwards by the secretary, who had brought a kettle, a packet of biscuits and a folding table. By the end of October the dairy was full. Crates were stacked to the ceiling, the piano sat under a sheet in the corner, and somebody had pinned a plan of the hall to the wall so that everyone could see where the new roof would go. The work itself began in the second week of November. Scaffolding went up and the slates came down in buckets, and the noise carried to the other end of the street from morning until dusk. The committee worried about the cost. The original estimate was well under the final bill, but the contractors found rot in two of the trusses and the figure climbed by a further twelve per cent. A grant application was submitted to the county, and a fund raising appeal was opened at the post office. Letters went to every household asking for whatever people could spare, and a box was placed by the till in the shop. The response was generous in a quiet way. Pensions and pocket money arrived in small envelopes, and the shop keeper added ten per cent of her takings on Saturdays. By Christmas the appeal had raised nine hundred pounds, which covered the rot and left a little over for paint. The roof was finished in January, and the committee planned a reopening for the last weekend of the month. They expected a crowd, since the whole village had followed the work from the pavement outside. The weather turned on the Friday and a gale blew down the street all night, so that the banners tied to the railings came loose and had to be retied in the morning. By the time the doors opened on the Saturday, only a handful of people had come, and most of those were the committee itself, standing by the tea urn in their coats. The chairman made a short speech, thanked the contractors, and declared the roof open. Everyone went home before lunch, and the dairy was cleared the following month, one crate at a time, in much the same way that it had been filled.
